text:
The Clean Shipping Coalition (CSC) has urged IMO member states to continue supporting the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) ahead of their next meeting. The framework, developed after lengthy negotiations, aims to meet the IMO’s climate goals. The CSC warns that alternative proposals could weaken climate protection in shipping.

CSC President Lukas Leppert describes the NZF, despite lower ambitions than hoped, as the best available solution. „The NZF has received broad political support from member states and must be adopted by the IMO in December,“ he says. Any further weakening would lead to a less effective and more costly transition.

Shipping accounts for 2-3% of global greenhouse gas emissions, roughly equivalent to Japan. The IMO aims for decarbonization by 2050, with interim targets of a 30% reduction by 2030 and 80% by 2040.

Discussions on the Net-Zero Framework

At ISWG-GHG 22 in London, the NZF and its potential adoption in December at MEPC 85/ES.2 are up for discussion. The framework approved at MEPC 83 in 2025 includes a global fuel standard. Ship operators are expected to gradually reduce emissions or pay penalties.

Delaine McCullough from Ocean Conservancy emphasizes the economic significance of shipping and its climate impact. It releases about one billion tons of carbon dioxide annually. Further delays are unacceptable.

The CSC considers proposals from Liberia and Japan unsuitable. Liberia would allow ships to use conventional fuels if cleaner alternatives are deemed too expensive or unavailable. Japan proposes payments to freely chosen projects instead of a central fund. According to Alex Springer from Transport & Environment, this could finance projects that hardly reduce emissions.

Need for Clear Regulation

The CSC demands that the IMO or an independent body centrally manage the fund. The resources should support a fair transition phase, especially for states heavily affected by climate change.

Leppert views the proposals from Liberia and Japan as a threat to climate protection in shipping. The IMO and its member states must protect and adopt the NZF in its current form.

text:
CPC Corporation, Taiwan's state-owned energy company, has announced plans to offer marine biofuel bunkering at Kaohsiung, with supplies of B24-VLSFO expected to begin reaching ships from October.

In an announcement made today, the company said it expects to provide B24-VLSFO to ships calling at the port starting next month.

"CPC Corporation, Taiwan, is pleased to announce that we will supply marine biofuel at Kaohsiung ports to align with global maritime net-zero greenhouse gas emissions targets and Taiwan's Net-Zoe Transition policy," the company said.

"We expect to provide B24 LSMF-180 (0.5%) bunkering services starting in October 2026."

B24 is a blend in which biofuel, typically fatty acid methyl esters derived from used cooking oil or other waste feedstocks, makes up 24% of the fuel, with the remainder being conventional very low sulfur fuel oil. Biofuel blends of this kind are already offered at other major Asian bunkering hubs, including Singapore, which has developed a significant marine biofuel market in recent years as shipowners seek fuels that can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions without requiring engine modifications.

The move comes as the shipping industry faces tightening international requirements, with the International Maritime Organization having adopted a revised greenhouse gas strategy in 2023 that includes goals of reaching net-zero emissions for international shipping by or around 2050, and the European Union's FuelEU Maritime regulation taking effect in 2025 to lower the greenhouse gas intensity of energy used by ships calling at EU ports.

According to CPC, the new service will give ships calling at Kaohsiung access to a lower-carbon marine fuel option as the shipping industry works to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions.

Beyond its planned biofuel offering, CPC Corporation supplies bunker fuels at several Taiwanese ports, including Kaohsiung, Taichung, Keelung, and Suao/Hualien. Kaohsiung is Taiwan's largest port and one of the major container gateways in the region, giving passing boxships and other vessels the option to refuel with the lower-carbon blend without deviating from their routes.

title: Cyprus Enters Fierce IMO Maritime Negotiations Over Global Shipping Carbon Emissions Levies
description:
The Republic of Cyprus has entered a highly consequential phase of global maritime negotiations in London, fiercely debating the implementation of a universal carbon pricing mechanism for the international shipping industry.
This legislation targets ocean-going ships exceeding 5,000 gross tonnage, an asset class responsible for over 85 percent of all international maritime emissions.
The Pricing Mechanism: A mandatory carbon levy applied to fuel consumption, designed to mathematically force fleet operators toward green alternatives.
The Cypriot Shipping Deputy Ministry argued that a narrowly backed, aggressive measure would prove operationally unworkable, risking global supply chain paralysis.
Global Supply Chain Repercussions The imposition of maritime carbon levies threatens to trigger a profound economic shockwave across African and Asian supply chains.
text:
The Republic of Cyprus has entered a highly consequential phase of global maritime negotiations in London, fiercely debating the implementation of a universal carbon pricing mechanism for the international shipping industry. As the International Maritime Organization (IMO) convenes its 22nd greenhouse gas working group session, billions of dollars hinge on the finalized architecture of the Net-Zero Fund.

The negotiations place Cyprus, boasting one of the European Union's most formidable maritime registries, at the absolute epicenter of a regulatory dispute that deeply fractured the EU last year. The upcoming directives will unequivocally determine the financial penalties for non-compliance and dictate the exact velocity at which commercial fleets must decarbonize.

The Net-Zero Framework and Financial Stakes

The proposed IMO framework seeks to establish the first globally mandated system combining strict limitations on the greenhouse gas intensity of marine fuels with a punitive pricing mechanism for deficient vessels. This legislation targets ocean-going ships exceeding 5,000 gross tonnage, an asset class responsible for over 85 percent of all international maritime emissions.

The Pricing Mechanism: A mandatory carbon levy applied to fuel consumption, designed to mathematically force fleet operators toward green alternatives.

The Net-Zero Fund: A multi-billion-dollar financial reservoir generated by the carbon taxes, intended to subsidize the research and development of sustainable maritime technologies.

The Operational Cost: Shipowners face massive capital expenditures to retrofit existing fleets or face crippling operational taxes that will inevitably be passed down the supply chain.

The Cyprus Shipping Chamber (CSC) has vigorously advocated for a universally standardized agreement, warning that a fragmented, regionalized taxation system would catastrophicly increase compliance costs and decimate the competitiveness of Mediterranean fleets.

The Diplomatic Divide

Cyprus and Greece fundamentally disrupted European consensus when they officially abstained from the IMO's extraordinary environmental session in late 2025, effectively postponing the formal adoption of the Net-Zero Framework. The Cypriot Shipping Deputy Ministry argued that a narrowly backed, aggressive measure would prove operationally unworkable, risking global supply chain paralysis.

The current four-day summit in London serves as the primary battleground to reconcile the ambitious environmental targets demanded by climate scientists with the harsh economic realities of global freight logistics. A secondary working group will convene in November to finalize the technical parameters before the ultimate vote in December.

Global Supply Chain Repercussions

The imposition of maritime carbon levies threatens to trigger a profound economic shockwave across African and Asian supply chains. If the IMO enacts a high-cost compliance model, vital cargo transit through Kenya's Port of Mombasa, Nigeria's Apapa complex, and major Australian export terminals will face immediate freight rate escalations. These increased maritime logistics costs will translate directly into higher consumer prices for imported energy, wheat, and fertilizer, fundamentally testing the economic resilience of developing nations reliant on globalized maritime trade.

text:
bound4blue has signed a repeat order with Odfjell, the leading deep-sea chemical tanker owner and operator, for the installation of eSAILs® on the 49,000 dwt chemical tanker Bow Optima. The retrofit, scheduled to take place in China in Q2 2027, follows the installation of bound4blue’s suction sails on sister vessel Bow Olympus in March 2025, reflecting Odfjell’s confidence in the technology as part of its fleet decarbonisation strategy.

Repeat confidence

Bow Optima operates in Odfjell’s round-the-world trade, supporting the safe and efficient transportation of liquids and chemicals for the company’s global customer base. The vessel has already been made wind-ready during a scheduled drydocking, with the installation of eSAIL® foundations, cabling and related deck ancillaries. The four 22m tall suction sails will be fitted to these foundations following delivery from bound4blue’s production facilities in China.

The new order builds on operational experience from Bow Olympus, where Odfjell has reported strong early performance from the vessel’s existing eSAIL® installation. According to Odfjell, Bow Olympus observed a 15-20% energy-saving effect in good, but not perfect, wind conditions, equivalent to approximately five tonnes of fuel saved per day and around 15 tonnes of CO2 emissions avoided per day. Odfjell has also reported fuel consumption reductions of up to 40% during operation.

Future-proofed fleet

The contract is Odfjell’s first repeat order with bound4blue and supports the company’s broader programme of deploying energy-saving technology across its fleet. Over the last decade, Odfjell has installed more than 140 energy-saving devices on its vessels, reducing carbon intensity by more than 53% compared with the International Maritime Organization’s 2008 baseline. The company is targeting a further improvement to 57% by 2030.

“Odfjell has taken a practical, data-led approach to vessel efficiency over many years, and Bow Olympus has given us valuable operational experience with wind-assisted propulsion in deep-sea chemical tanker trades,” says Erik Hjortland, VP Technology at Odfjell. “The documented results from the first installation have strengthened our confidence in continuing with wind propulsion on selected vessels. Bow Optima is a natural next step, and the project supports our wider objective of reducing fuel consumption, emissions and exposure to future cost pressures.”

Building tanker momentum

bound4blue’s eSAIL® is a fully automated suction sail technology that uses an aerodynamically optimised structure and active airflow control to generate additional propulsive force from wind. This allows the vessel to reduce engine load under suitable operating conditions, lowering fuel consumption and associated emissions. The system is designed to operate autonomously, minimising additional workload for crew, and can be integrated into both retrofit and newbuild projects.

As of today, bound4blue has deployed eSAIL® systems on thirteen ships, with five more in its order book, representing more than 50 eSAILs®, with 10 installations completed or contracted for the tanker segment.

For chemical tanker operators, wind-assisted propulsion can provide a direct efficiency measure that works alongside existing propulsion systems, route optimisation, alternative fuels and other onboard energy-saving technologies. By reducing fuel consumption, it can also help owners limit exposure to fuel price volatility and carbon-related costs, including under frameworks such as the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime.

Scaling wind-assisted propulsion adoption

“Odfjell’s repeat order is rooted in real operating experience, not just future ambition,” comments José Miguel Bermúdez, CEO and co-founder at bound4blue. “Bow Olympus demonstrated how suction sail technology can contribute to meaningful fuel savings in the demanding environment of deep-sea chemical tanker operations, and Bow Optima shows how that learning can be carried into further fleet deployment. We value the consolidated partnership with Odfjell, whose disciplined approach to decarbonisation and performance monitoring is exactly what the market needs as wind-assisted propulsion moves from first projects to repeat adoption.”

The two-phase approach on Bow Optima also illustrates how owners can prepare vessels for wind-assisted propulsion installation during scheduled yard periods. By completing foundation and cabling work in advance, Odfjell has reduced the scope required for the planned Q2 2027 sail installation, supporting a more efficient retrofit process when the eSAILs® are delivered.

The order adds to growing market evidence that wind propulsion is moving into repeat deployment among owners assessing practical pathways to lower fuel use and emissions.

bound4blue’s eSAILs® generate forward thrust up to seven times greater than conventional rigid sails of the same size. The mechanically simple, non-ATEX units are suitable for a broad range of vessel types, including tankers, bulkers, ro-ros, cruise vessels, ferries, gas carriers, and general cargo vessels.

description:
Rolls-Royce has introduced an exhaust after-treatment system designed to bring its mtu Series 2000 marine engines into compliance with International Maritime Organization Tier III emissions requirements.
The system uses an aqueous urea solution to convert nitrogen oxides in the engine exhaust into nitrogen and water.
“With this new offering, all models in the mtu Series 2000 are now available with integrated SCR systems,” said Lukas Köhler, senior vice president, global marine and mining, Rolls-Royce Power Systems.
“We have already launched a new, flexible and compact solution for the more powerful mtu Series 4000.
The addition completes Rolls-Royce’s Tier III after-treatment portfolio for its primary mtu marine propulsion engine lines.
text:
Rolls-Royce has introduced an exhaust after-treatment system designed to bring its mtu Series 2000 marine engines into compliance with International Maritime Organization Tier III emissions requirements.

Developed with exhaust after-treatment specialist Eminox, the selective catalytic reduction system will allow offshore supply vessels, ferries, crewboats and patrol boats powered by Series 2000 engines to operate in emission control areas, including the North Sea and Baltic Sea.

The system uses an aqueous urea solution to convert nitrogen oxides in the engine exhaust into nitrogen and water. Rolls-Royce said it reduces nitrogen oxide emissions by 75% compared with IMO Tier II limits.

“With this new offering, all models in the mtu Series 2000 are now available with integrated SCR systems,” said Lukas Köhler, senior vice president, global marine and mining, Rolls-Royce Power Systems. “We have already launched a new, flexible and compact solution for the more powerful mtu Series 4000. This enables us to equip our customers with future-proof propulsion systems to meet the challenges of modern shipping.”

Depending on the engine’s load profile, the Series 2000 after-treatment system is designed for a service life of up to 16,000 operating hours. The system does not require compressed air for urea dosing and can be configured for installation in a range of vessel designs.

The addition completes Rolls-Royce’s Tier III after-treatment portfolio for its primary mtu marine propulsion engine lines.

title: From first movers to mass adoption: making the IMO Net-Zero goal achievable - IMarEST
description:
The choice of reward mechanism will need to balance value for money with the certainty needed to unlock investment and encourage early adoption.
Details of the framework are still under discussion, but options include the creation of a Net-Zero Fund.
If that is not possible, they would pay into the Net-Zero Fund (Remedial Units).
Finding the right reward price One of the distribution options being explored is reverse auctions.
Reverse auctions could help the IMO discover what reward the market needs, while making efficient use of limited fund revenues.
text:
The design options of the IMO’s proposed Net-Zero Framework and consequential Net-Zero Fund could be critical to turning early investment in zero- and near-zero-emission fuels into a self-sustaining market. The choice of reward mechanism will need to balance value for money with the certainty needed to unlock investment and encourage early adoption.

For the last few years, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has been working towards adoption of its Net-Zero Framework, a set of regulations aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions from ships over 5,000 gross tonnage.

Details of the framework are still under discussion, but options include the creation of a Net-Zero Fund. Ships that exceed emissions thresholds would need to rebalance their emissions through emission credit trading (Surplus Units), such as between ships. If that is not possible, they would pay into the Net-Zero Fund (Remedial Units).

“The revenues should be used for rewarding users of zero- and near-zero-emission fuels (ZNZs), and for just and equitable transition purposes that support the needs of low-income countries,” says Dr Tristan Smith (FIMarEST), Professor of Energy and Transport at University College London and part of the IMarEST delegation to the IMO.

The question is how that money could be distributed equitably so that net-zero goals are reached in line with the agreed 2023 IMO GHG strategy on reduction of GHG emissions from ships.

Finding the right reward price

One of the distribution options being explored is reverse auctions.

“A reverse auction is a standard tool that is used quite frequently in policy to get a certain amount of subsidy or support into a market in the most competitive way possible,” Smith says.

In brief, “the IMO would set up an auction window, and the market would say what price they would need as a subsidy in order to operate on ZNZs, and the IMO would allocate the money to those who had the lowest price.” Because the auction allocates a pre-determined amount of the fund’s revenues, it can guarantee a reward rate for a period of time into the future.

The alternative solution would be a fixed price option. “Instead of going to the market and saying, what price do you need, the IMO would say ‘we think if we set the subsidy at this rate, the market will be able to use it in order to create the use of ZNZs that we’re trying to stimulate,” Smith explains.

However, this mechanism then needs to be able to manage the situation where there is more demand for these fixed rewards than there are funds available – with current options under consideration removing the certainty that the stated reward rate is what will be paid out in practice.

Each mechanism has trade-offs. Reverse auctions could help the IMO discover what reward the market needs, while making efficient use of limited fund revenues. Fixed-price rewards could give shipowners and fuel suppliers a simpler mechanism to interface with, but depend on setting the right rate: too low, and they may not unlock early ZNZ fuel use; too high, and the fund risks overpaying and/or producing uncertainty in the actual reward rate that can be paid out.

However, “you don't have to go one way or the other. You can use them both in combination,” explains Smith, pointing to support for the emerging renewable energy in the UK. “We had some portions of the market that were well serviced by just having a flat rate and other portions that needed something that could provide a certainty of reward price and a more competitive process for deriving that price.”

Regardless of the route taken, the reward mechanism should ensure that Net-Zero Fund revenues support technical solutions that can deliver meaningful emissions reductions, be deployed in practice, and are accessible to developed and developing economies alike. Funding should prioritise long-term, scalable solutions that help establish the fuel supply chains, infrastructure, and market confidence necessary to accelerate widespread adoption across the global shipping industry.

Early support to grow the market

Whichever option, or mix of options, is chosen, the reward mechanism is seen by many as key to scaling ZNZs. As Smith notes, “the core of the Net-Zero Framework” is the appropriate policy design requiring the “decreasing carbon intensity over time of the energy used on board ships.”

The reward mechanism is intended to support those ready to move first. “If you’re a shipowner who wants to be an early adopter, you’ve got the reward mechanism to help make your business case in the early years,” Smith says. Others may wait for a variety of reasons, following a more “gradual curve” of adoption as the market develops in large part due to those early adopters. “It allows multiple compliance strategies in practice,” says Smith.

Indeed, creating a global supply chain is neither easy nor cheap. A green ammonia production facility, Smith notes, can cost around $10 billion to build. “No one’s going to find easy ways to raise that capital without being able to say, yes, I’ve got an order book that’s already full.” Producers and others in the supply chain need confidence that buyers will exist before investing in production and development. Shipowners need confidence that fuels will be available, affordable, and usable before committing to them.

“The reward mechanism needs to support early adoption, which may initially mean supporting someone who only buys fuel in one of the major ports, but it then needs to be able to help ZNZ to be rolled out in a geographically inclusive way to have widely available supply.”

For Smith, success would be measured not only by the first ships using ZNZ fuels, but by the investment curve behind them. “Transitions often happen by starting with very small volumes, which makes them tractable, before they reach some sort of tipping point,” he explains.

In the case of shipping, that tipping point is linked to the IMO target for 5% of the sector’s energy to come from ZNZ fuels. “After that tipping point, you're starting to generate something which becomes self-fulfilling. So as long as there are no obstructions to it, the ramp up becomes faster and faster until you get to mass market adoption.”

Discussions at the IMO are set to continue later this year, with the reward mechanism still to be worked through. IMarEST will continue to contribute technical input on the Net Zero Framework policy design and guidelines including at the upcoming MEPC (Marine Environment Protection Committee) 85 meeting in late 2026.

text:
Ardent Energy, a leading UK and Netherlands producer of waste-based biodiesel, insists that postponed regulation must not translate into stalled progress.

It said that the the industry already has viable alternative fuels that can deliver meaningful emissions reductions today.

“The industry must not stand still,” said Dickon Posnett, corporate affairs director at Argent Energy.

“The IMO’s efforts remain vital, but regulatory delays should not deter shipping companies from acting now. Solutions exist now. Companies can act now.”

Biodiesel alternative

Argent Energy is advocating for the wider use of waste-derived biodiesel as a marine fuel.

These drop-in biofuels can be used in existing ships without modification, providing an immediate path to lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Its Argent SeaFuel product, made exclusively from waste-based feedstocks, is already being used on multiple European routes and meets stringent sustainability standards.

The company owns one of several biodiesel plants operational in the Port of Amsterdam.

Argent Energy said biofuels align with both the IMO’s Net-Zero Framework and the EU’s FuelEU Maritime Regulation, making them a key tool for short-term marine decarbonisation.

“The climate crisis isn’t waiting, and neither should we,” added Mr Posnett. “No single country or interest group should hold back global progress.”

Argent Energy said it will continue to work with shipowners, ports and regulators to accelerate the transition to cleaner marine fuel and sustain momentum toward zero emissions.

A shipping industry that manages the transition successfully protects the jobs and trade flows that countries depend on, making the case for investment as much an economic argument as an environmental one.
text:
Opening one of shipping’s most closely watched global gatherings, the International Maritime Organization’s Secretary-General used the SMM stage to deliver a pointed message to the industry: don’t judge IMO’s priorities by what makes the news. In a wide-ranging address that touched on decarbonisation, alternative fuels, global regulation, and the need for broader industry engagement, the Secretary-General pushed back against the perception that decarbonisation has slipped down the agenda simply because it has faded from headlines.

Why doesn’t decarbonisation dominate headlines anymore?

The Secretary-General opened by directly addressing a narrative that has circulated in shipping circles this year, the idea that decarbonisation has cooled as a priority because it no longer commands the same media attention it once did. Drawing a parallel to safety, the address noted that IMO devotes enormous resources to safety and security work that rarely surfaces in headlines either, yet no one would argue safety has become less important as a result.

The point was framed as a broader caution against equating visibility with substance. Headlines, the Secretary-General said, function as an opening for the organisation to keep reinforcing why shipping matters globally, how deeply interconnected the sector is, and how it underpins the daily lives of people around the world. But headline volume was explicitly separated from the actual scale of work happening inside IMO across its many technical and policy tracks. The message to delegates was straightforward: the absence of a topic from the news cycle is not evidence of institutional neglect.

Where do global emissions regulations currently stand?

Turning to the regulatory track, the Secretary-General acknowledged that the pace of global rulemaking has drawn criticism, and reframed the delay as a natural consequence of how consequential the outcome is. The observation that “everyone wants a piece of it” was used to explain why reaching consensus among IMO’s member states takes time when the stakes, covering fuel standards, emissions pricing, and compliance mechanisms for a truly global fleet, are this high.

The Secretary-General also addressed the elephant in the room for many delegates: the European Union’s decision to move ahead with its own regional framework, including emissions trading obligations for shipping, ahead of a global IMO agreement. Rather than treating this as a setback, the address characterised it as one example among several, noting that the EU’s own path has not been without friction. The clear signal was that IMO does not view regional first-movers as undermining the case for a global framework, but as one data point in a broader process that continues to move forward regardless.

Concretely, the Secretary-General revealed that the next round of IMO negotiations on the topic had opened barely an hour before the SMM address, underscoring that the regulatory track remains actively in motion even when it is not generating headlines.

What role does early investment play in the fuel transition?

A significant portion of the address was devoted to a direct appeal to industry and government alike: invest now, ahead of returns, or risk being left behind when the transition accelerates. The Secretary-General cited India as an example worth following, pointing to capital already flowing into green technologies, alternative fuels, and shipbuilding capacity well ahead of any guaranteed payoff.

This was framed as the model IMO wants to see replicated more broadly. Alternative fuels, the address noted, are not a theoretical proposition. The underlying technologies and fuel types have already been developed. What has not yet happened is scale. Getting fuels like ammonia, methanol, and other alternatives from pilot projects to fleet-wide adoption requires the kind of early capital commitment that only pays off once volumes rise and costs fall, a dynamic familiar from other energy transitions.

On the safety side of that same transition, the Secretary-General pointed to concrete IMO deliverables already in place, including guidelines issued for the use of ammonia as a marine propulsion fuel, a necessary regulatory foundation given ammonia’s toxicity and handling risks compared to conventional bunker fuel. Work has also begun on nuclear propulsion, which the Secretary-General described as now high on the agenda for the sector, reflecting growing industry interest in next-generation power sources for large vessels as decarbonisation targets tighten.

Who else needs a seat at the table?

Perhaps the most striking part of the address was its emphasis on who shipping needs to be listening to, rather than what it needs to be building. The Secretary-General was explicit that IMO does not expect to solve the sector’s challenges from within its own membership alone. Solutions, the address argued, will require sustained engagement with the energy sector, organised labour, environmental groups, and technology developers, alongside the traditional shipowner and flag-state constituencies that have historically driven IMO’s agenda.

Two groups were singled out by name: the younger generation entering the industry, and seafarers themselves, who the Secretary-General said should have a greater voice in shaping the policies that will define their working lives at sea. This is a notable shift in framing for an organisation often associated with government delegations and shipowner associations, and it signals an intent to widen participation beyond the traditional IMO negotiating table.

Governments and ministries were also called on to engage more actively, not simply as regulators but as enablers, using incentive structures to support the sector’s transition rather than relying solely on mandates.

What’s the economic case for a secure, sustainable shipping sector?

Closing the address, the Secretary-General connected the decarbonisation and safety agendas back to a broader economic argument. Shipping, the address noted, is a major global employer, and demonstrating that the sector can be both secure and sustainable is itself a tool for supporting economies around the world. A shipping industry that manages the transition successfully protects the jobs and trade flows that countries depend on, making the case for investment as much an economic argument as an environmental one.

The Secretary-General ended on a note of shared responsibility rather than institutional ownership, making clear that IMO alone cannot deliver on the scale of change required. Running short on time, the address closed with a direct acknowledgment that the path ahead depends on collective action across the sector, not decisions made unilaterally by the organisation itself.

The takeaway for SMM delegates

The address set a clear tone for this year’s SMM: decarbonisation has not been deprioritised, it has simply moved from headline-grabbing announcements into the harder, slower work of negotiation, technical standard-setting, and investment mobilisation. For an industry gathered to take stock of where shipping stands on its energy transition, the Secretary-General’s message was as much a challenge as a reassurance, urging delegates to invest ahead of certainty and to widen the circle of voices shaping shipping’s next chapter.

text:
The government has set a target to raise the number of green-certified ship recycling yards in the country to at least three digits (100+), Industries and Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said Sunday, noting that around 31 such yards currently exist while several more are undergoing green certification.

Muktadir made the remarks as chief guest at a workshop jointly organised by the Ministry of Industries and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) at a hotel in Dhaka’s Karwan Bazar. The workshop was held to discuss a feasibility study report on setting up a Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility (TSDF) centre under the “Bangladesh Safe and Environment-Friendly Ship Recycling Project.”

Muktadir said Bangladesh remains one of the world’s leading countries in ship recycling, having once surpassed even India in tonnage terms. Although the country has slipped somewhat in recent times, he said, it still holds a significant position in the global ship recycling industry.

Calling the sector vital to the national economy, the minister said it provides employment for a large number of people, while scrap from ships serves as a key raw material source for the country’s steel industry. He stressed that the sector’s growth must be ensured in a responsible and environment-friendly manner, adding that the government’s goal is to make the industry more modern, safe and sustainable through compliance with international conventions and environmental standards. To take the number of green-certified yards to a hundred-plus, the minister emphasised technical and financial support alongside effective enforcement of environmental compliance requirements.

Describing hazardous waste management as one of the biggest challenges in ship recycling, Muktadir said large ships generate various hazardous materials and waste during dismantling, which, if not properly managed, pose risks to the environment and public health. He said the proposed TSDF would play a key role in safely and scientifically collecting, storing, treating and disposing of such waste. The proposed facility is expected to handle a major share of hazardous waste from the ship recycling industry, while also creating scope for managing hazardous waste from other industrial sources, including e-waste.

The minister expressed hope that the facility would help align the sector with international environmental standards and enhance Bangladesh’s competitiveness in the global market, saying a coordinated effort involving the government, yard owners, relevant institutions and international partners could transform the ship recycling sector into a safer, more modern and sustainable industry.

The talks place Cyprus, one of Europe’s leading maritime states, at the centre of a dispute that divided the European Union last year.

A second working-group session is scheduled for November 23 to 27, followed by MEPC 85 from November 30 to December 3. The extraordinary session postponed last year is expected to resume on December 4, subject to confirmation.

description:

The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) today released its report, Quantity assurance in marine biofuel supply chains, outlining a practical approach to help shipowners verify that they receive both the total quantity of fuel and the renewable content contracted.
The approach draws on evidence from GCMD’s end-to-end marine biofuel supply chain trials conducted under commercial operating conditions.
Biofuels are purchased not only for their energy content, but also for the renewable content and emissions reductions they represent.
Verifying the renewable fraction in biofuel blends Verifying the renewable fraction requires appropriate analytical methods.
text:
As marine biofuel use scales, quantity assurance must account for both the delivered volume and its renewable fraction.

GCMD proposes a practical approach to distinguish normal measurement variation from potential under-blending.

The report completes GCMD’s quality, quantity, and GHG emissions abatement assurance framework for marine biofuels.

The Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation (GCMD) today released its report, Quantity assurance in marine biofuel supply chains, outlining a practical approach to help shipowners verify that they receive both the total quantity of fuel and the renewable content contracted. The approach draws on evidence from GCMD’s end-to-end marine biofuel supply chain trials conducted under commercial operating conditions.

Biofuels are purchased not only for their energy content, but also for the renewable content and emissions reductions they represent. The renewable fraction determines the green premium and underpins GHG accounting and regulatory compliance, yet blend ratios, such as B24 or B30, are typically supplier-declared rather than independently verified. Closing this verification gap will strengthen confidence in marine biofuel transactions.

Ensuring reliable measurement of total quantity transferred

Mass flow meters (MFMs) have become the preferred method for custody transfer, as they provide a transparent and auditable basis for determining the quantity of fuel transferred. However, adding fatty acid methyl ester (FAME) to conventional marine fuels, such as Very Low Sulphur Fuel Oil (VLSFO) or High Sulphur Fuel Oil (HSFO), can reduce the final blend’s viscosity, potentially pushing it outside the validated operating range of the MFM installed on the bunker barge. To maintain measurement integrity, the viscosity of the final blend should therefore be assessed under the actual transfer conditions against the applicable MFM operating range. This can be managed through appropriate transfer-temperature control or by using MFMs that have been validated for broader ranges.

Verifying the renewable fraction in biofuel blends

Verifying the renewable fraction requires appropriate analytical methods. FAME-based blends can be verified through compositional analysis, while hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO)-based blends require radiocarbon analysis because renewable and fossil hydrocarbons cannot be distinguished through compositional testing.

Interpreting analytical measurements, however, is not straightforward. Neat FAME may contain up to 3.5% non-ester material, so the measurable FAME content of a finished BXX blend may not exactly match its declared blend ratio.

Laboratory methods also have finite measurement precision. A difference between a measured result and a declared blend ratio therefore does not necessarily indicate incorrect blending or under-delivery.

Completing GCMD’s three-pillar biofuels assurance framework

Together, the three pillars of GCMD’s quality, quantity, and GHG emissions abatement assurance framework address whether the fuel is fit for use, delivers the claimed emissions reductions, and contains the contracted fuel quantity and renewable content.

Professor Lynn Loo, CEO of GCMD, said, “Buyers need confidence that they have received both the fuel and the renewable content they paid for. This report provides a practical, evidence-backed basis for verifying renewable fuel claims, protecting commercial value and supporting credible GHG accounting as marine biofuel use scales.”

title: Cyprus faces fresh IMO battle over shipping emissions

text:
Cyprus enters a decisive four-day round of global shipping talks in London on Tuesday, as member states seek agreement on rules that will determine how quickly ships must cut emissions, what non-compliance will cost and whether billions of dollars will pass through a new Net-Zero Fund.

The negotiations place Cyprus, one of Europe’s leading maritime states, back at the centre of a dispute that divided the European Union last year.

Cyprus and Greece abstained when the International Maritime Organisation’s (IMO) extraordinary environmental session voted in October 2025 to postpone formal adoption of the Net-Zero Framework for one year. The measure had been approved in April but was not adopted, leaving its future open to further negotiation.

The Shipping Deputy Ministry subsequently explained that Cyprus had sought to create room for a broader agreement, supporting an IMO framework that was both ambitious and workable. A narrowly backed measure, it argued, could prove difficult to implement and encourage more regional rules.

The Cyprus Shipping Chamber (CSC) has also supported a global agreement, warning that fragmented regional requirements would increase costs and weaken competitiveness. As the chamber has previously stressed, “only global rules can decarbonise a global industry”.

The 22nd session of the IMO’s working group on greenhouse gas emissions, known as ISWG-GHG 22, runs from September 1 to 4. It is the first of two negotiating rounds intended to narrow the differences before the IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee meets later this year.

According to the IMO timetable, a second working-group session will follow from November 23 to 27, before MEPC 85 meets from November 30 to December 3. The extraordinary session postponed last year is expected to resume on December 4, subject to confirmation.

The London talks will not settle the issue, but they will show whether an agreement in December remains possible. The IMO said in May that close to 100 delegations had set out their positions, prompting secretary-general Arsenio Dominguez to say the organisation was “back on track”, although it still had to “rebuild trust”.

The framework would create the first global system combining mandatory limits on the greenhouse gas intensity of marine fuels with a pricing mechanism for ships that fail to meet them.

It would apply to oceangoing vessels above 5,000 gross tonnage, which account for more than 85 per cent of emissions from international shipping.

Compliance would be measured through GHG Fuel Intensity, or GFI, expressed in grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per megajoule of energy. The calculation would cover carbon dioxide, methane and nitrous oxide across the entire fuel lifecycle, from production and transport to use on board.

This well-to-wake method is particularly important for LNG because methane released during production, transport or combustion can substantially increase the fuel’s final emissions rating.

Under the approved draft, ships would face two compliance tiers. The base target would initially require a 4 per cent reduction in fuel-emission intensity in 2028, rising to 30 per cent in 2035, compared with the 2008 average.

The stricter direct-compliance target would begin with a 17 per cent reduction and rise to 43 per cent over the same period. These dates are now expected to change because adoption was delayed.

Ships exceeding the limits could use surplus units bought from better-performing vessels, draw on units saved from previous years or acquire remedial units by contributing to the IMO Net-Zero Fund.

The initial prices in the draft were set at $100 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent for a Tier 1 shortfall and $380 for Tier 2 during the 2028-2030 reporting periods. Ships performing better than the direct-compliance target could earn units to sell or retain for later use.

Revenue from the pricing mechanism would finance rewards for zero- and near-zero-emission fuels, along with research, infrastructure, training, technology transfer and support for developing countries. Estimates suggest the original framework could raise around $10 billion a year, making the Fund’s governance and allocation among the most politically sensitive issues in the talks.

Four proposed amendments were circulated within the six-month period required under the MARPOL convention. A fifth approach, submitted later by Japan as a paper for MEPC 85, will also form part of the negotiations, although its timing creates a legal complication if members seek to use it as the basis for adoption in December.

Australia, Canada, South Africa and the United Kingdom propose retaining the framework almost unchanged, with the dates moved back to account for the one-year delay. Their proposal keeps both compliance tiers, the remedial and surplus units and the Net-Zero Fund.

Brazil retains the same broad structure but proposes a gentler start, followed by stronger requirements later. Its plan would delay the early GFI reductions by about two years before increasing the 2040 base reduction from 65 to 70 per cent.

Brazil also proposes replacing the Fund with a lighter facility that could work through accredited international institutions. Supporters say this would reduce early compliance pressure while fuel production and bunkering infrastructure expand. Critics argue that delaying the tougher requirements would also delay investment in cleaner fuels.

Tuvalu takes the strictest approach. Its proposal would effectively place a charge on all remaining ship emissions, remove the opportunity to generate surplus units and increase the Tier 1 price from $100 to $300 per tonne. The Tier 2 price would remain at $380.

The proposal is supported by a group of Pacific island states seeking a stronger price signal for producers of green ammonia, methanol, hydrogen and synthetic fuels, as well as greater revenue for vulnerable developing countries.

Liberia proposes the most extensive redesign. It would link future tightening of the fuel standard to whether lower-emission fuels were commercially available, affordable and capable of being produced at scale.

Its system would depend more heavily on the trading, banking and borrowing of surplus units while removing mandatory contributions to an IMO-managed fund. A related submission from Liberia and Panama would allow ships to earn surplus units through verified energy-efficiency improvements, expanding recognition beyond fuel switching to measures that reduce actual consumption.

Japan has sought a middle course, retaining two compliance tiers while setting lower targets through 2035 and making later reductions dependent on the commercial availability of fuels and technologies.

Its proposal would remove mandatory payments and the Net-Zero Fund, relying more on surplus-unit trading. Companies could instead make direct contributions to eligible IMO-approved projects. However, because Japan’s proposal was not among the four amendments circulated within the MARPOL deadline, using it as the legal basis for immediate adoption could delay the process into 2027.

Recent independent modelling submitted to the working group by the Institute of Marine Engineering, Science and Technology found that Tuvalu’s levy-based option produced the deepest emissions cuts and was the only one of the four formally circulated amendments likely to meet the IMO’s 2030 and 2040 checkpoints.

The modelling found that retaining the existing framework offered the lowest average cost of cutting carbon among the three options that kept an emissions-pricing mechanism. Liberia’s redesign produced the weakest emissions result and no revenue for a just transition.

The European Union has signalled that it is prepared to consider changes, but its joint submission sets clear limits.

Any agreement must still lead to net-zero emissions by or around 2050 on a well-to-wake basis, encourage the transition from the first year, remain enforceable and provide credible financing for developing states. The EU has also accepted that flexibility may be needed where ships cannot obtain lower-emission fuels at the ports they visit.

However, tensions remain within Europe. Greek shipping minister Vassilis Kikilias warned before the meeting that preparatory discussions had not shown enough flexibility and had failed to give sufficient weight to member states representing more than 70 per cent of European shipping.

According to the Greek minister of Maritime Affairs and Insular Policy, Vassilis Kikilias, emission rules must reflect the actual development of fuels, propulsion systems and available technologies, without passing excessive costs to households and businesses.

The concern is particularly strong in bulk and tramp shipping, where vessels do not operate on fixed routes and cannot know years in advance which ports they will use or whether suitable fuels will be available.

Union of Greek Shipowners president Melina Travlou has described the Liberia-Panama approach as a more balanced basis for further discussion, although she said it could still be improved. She argued that fuel availability and affordability must be taken into account and that energy efficiency should be recognised as a direct means of reducing emissions.

The shipowners’ position reflects the central disagreement in London. If the IMO sets demanding targets before green fuels are produced at sufficient scale, ships may face high charges for fuels they cannot obtain. If the targets simply follow what is already available, producers may lack the guaranteed demand needed to invest in new plants.

The final rules will also have commercial consequences beyond the fuel bill. Responsibility for choosing the fuel, route and speed often lies with the charterer rather than the vessel owner, meaning compliance costs are likely to be addressed through charter-party clauses, management agreements and freight rates.

More efficient ships could gain commercial value through lower costs and the sale of surplus units. Older vessels with high consumption could face higher charges, reduced employment or pressure for early replacement.

Member states must still agree on fuel certification, traceability, methane calculations, the treatment of biofuels and recognition of wind-assisted propulsion. They must also complete the digital GFI Registry that will record each ship’s emissions, compliance balance and unit transactions.

The IMO’s wider climate strategy seeks net-zero emissions from international shipping by or around 2050. It calls for total emissions to fall by at least 20 per cent by 2030, while aiming for 30 per cent, followed by a reduction of at least 70 per cent by 2040, while aiming for 80 per cent, compared with 2008.

The question in London is therefore no longer whether shipping must cut emissions. It is whether countries can agree on a system strong enough to create a market for cleaner fuels while remaining workable for ships operating across different trades, routes and financial conditions.

text:
The emergence of “shadow fleets”, clandestine maritime networks designed to circumvent sanctions, poses a critical challenge to global maritime governance, safety, and environmental protection. This paper examines the regulatory response of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) to this phenomenon. It argues that, despite establishing a comprehensive framework through conventions such as the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), the IMO’s approach remains reactive and fragmented. The Maritime Labour Convention (MLC) is also considered in light of its relevance to seafarers’ rights. The study demonstrates that shadow fleets engage in systematic violations, including AIS manipulation, illicit ship-to-ship transfers, and the operation of aging and poorly maintained vessels, thereby increasing risks to maritime safety, environmental protection, and labor welfare. The analysis demonstrates that these patterns persist due to structural constraints, including the non-binding nature of key instruments, uneven flag state enforcement, and the technical limitations of the IMO’s mandate. In response, the paper proposes a more integrated governance model, including a precautionary exercise of the IMO’s mandate, strengthened enforcement through targeted audits and transparency measures, enhanced coordination with other regimes such as the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) and the International Labour Organization (ILO), and clarification of the role of coastal states within the exclusive economic zone (EEZ). This research contributes to the field of maritime governance by bridging policy-oriented analyses of shadow fleet operations with legal scholarship, offering a political economy explanation for persistent non-compliance and providing policy-relevant insights for mitigating associated risks.

text:
Stronger global regulatory changes will accelerate the uptake of low greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions marine fuels, classification society DNV said in the 10th edition of its report ‘Maritime Forecast to 2050’.

IMAGE: ENGINE via ChatGPT

Global maritime industry’s demand for low-GHG fuels is expected to range from 4-22 million mt of oil equivalent (Mtoe) by 2030 and 33-185 Mtoe by 2050, depending on the regulatory path the International Maritime Organization (IMO) ultimately takes.

The report models four regulatory scenarios, from adoption of the IMO's Net-Zero Framework (NZF) in its current form to its outright rejection, which DNV said could trigger a prolonged regulatory gridlock.

The wide range reflects the industry's fuel-switching pace – directly linked to regulatory outcomes, the future uptake of shore power, plug-in hybridisation, nuclear power, and onboard carbon capture systems, DNV said.

Current project pipelines will supply up to 270 Mtoe of low-GHG fuel by 2030, actual volumes are likely to come in lower because of project delays and other uncertainties, and shipping will be competing with other sectors for the same fuel, the classification society added.

By testing fuel and technology choices against multiple regulatory scenarios, shipowners can find strategies that hold up as regulation, fuel availability, prices, and technologies evolve, lead author of the report Øyvind Sekkesæter said.

Efficiency as a shield against regulatory whims

DNV also said shipowners can use energy efficiency as a lever, regardless of how the regulatory picture settles.

A case study of a hydrodynamic retrofit on a 5,000 TEU vessel projected potential annual fuel savings of 16%, with a payback period of around one to four years depending on future fuel prices. DNV said such retrofits can typically be completed during a standard class-renewal dry-docking.

“Ships ordered today will operate well beyond 2050, but many of the factors shaping their future performance remain uncertain,” DNV's maritime chief executive Cristina Saenz de Santa Maria said.

With strong global regulatory changes and advanced energy efficient technology in place, the world fleet could consume up to 25% less energy by 2050 than under a scenario where regulation is driven mainly by regions, according to DNV.

The cost of cutting emissions varies widely by fuel pathway, DNV said, with abatement costs ranging from about $180/mt to $1,290/mt of CO2 avoided.

“Regulatory requirements are advancing faster than the fuel, infrastructure, and technological systems needed to support them, making long-term investment decisions increasingly complex,” DNV's maritime chief executive added.

text:
Mitsubishi Shipbuilding a part of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Group, has received an order from Hitachi Zosen Marine Engine for its MAmmoSS® ammonia fuel handling system.

HZME is a dual licensee of Everllence SE and WinGD, major licensors of marine engines. MAmmoSS® will be designed and optimized to be compatible with the ammonia marine engines of these two licensors, and after delivery to HZME’s facility, will be used for shop tests of both engines.

The International Maritime Organization (IMO)’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) has been engaged in ongoing discussions on reducing greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from international shipping. The MEPC 80 session adopted the 2023 IMO Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships, which aims to reach net-zero GHG emissions from international shipping by 2050, while MEPC 83 approved mid-term measures to reduce GHG emissions.

Decarbonization in global shipping is a critical issue, and ammonia, which does not emit CO2 when burned, is attracting attention as a next-generation marine fuel that will significantly contribute to reducing GHG emissions in the shipping industry. However, as ammonia is a toxic fluid, safe handling technology onboard ships is essential and is expected to drive demand for MAmmoSS®.

Going forward, Mitsubishi Shipbuilding will continue to provide safe and reliable products for ammonia-fueled vessels to support the expected market expansion, while also enhancing functionality and deliver greater value to meet the diverse needs of customers.

text:
WASHINGTON — Perpetual Next, a Dutch climate technology and renewable energy company, has commissioned Kreston ME Consulting to conduct a feasibility study for a proposed biomethanol production facility and regional commercial platform in the United Arab Emirates.

The study will assess whether the project is commercially, financially and technically viable, with Abu Dhabi identified as the preferred location for evaluation. The final site and development approach will depend on the study’s findings.

The reference project would produce approximately 220,000 metric tons of biomethanol annually using about 320,000 metric tons of imported biocarbon made from sustainable residues, Perpetual Next said in a press release.

Kreston ME Consulting, which is based in Dubai in the UAE, will assess regional and international demand, potential buyers, permitting and regulatory requirements, industrial sites, utilities, port infrastructure and feedstock-import logistics.

The study also will examine estimated capital and operating costs, possible financing and investment structures, development risks and the steps needed to prepare the project for investment.

The companies expect the work to be completed in the fourth quarter of 2026.

“The UAE represents a compelling potential location within Perpetual Next’s international development strategy,” Anthony Mayle, the company’s head of business development, said in a statement.

Mayle cited the UAE’s shipping connections, industrial and energy infrastructure, and efforts to develop lower-carbon fuels. He said the assessment would support discussions with potential industrial partners, investors and lenders.

KMEC said it would combine its local market, regulatory and infrastructure expertise with capabilities from the Kreston Global network. The consultancy plans to engage industrial zones, infrastructure providers and market participants to test the project’s assumptions.

“We are pleased to support Perpetual Next as it evaluates the UAE as a potential location for its biomethanol platform,” Govind Menon, a growth strategist at KMEC, said in a statement.

Perpetual Next said the proposed UAE facility would support its broader plan to develop an international network of renewable-carbon and biomethanol production assets.

Biomethanol can serve as a lower-carbon alternative to conventional methanol in industries including maritime transport and chemicals, according to the company.

Perpetual Next is developing large-scale facilities in the Netherlands, Estonia and the United States, the company said.

It did not disclose the estimated cost, financing arrangements or potential construction date for the UAE project.

text:
Ammobia Inc. (San Francisco, Calif.), a developer of breakthrough low-cost, modular ammonia production technology, announced an agreement with Lummus Technology LLC (Houston, Texas) to license and deploy Ammobia’s ammonia production system. Through this partnership, Ammobia’s production technology is to be deployed in commercial installations worldwide and used in integrated solutions that complement Lummus’ hydrogen portfolio, including marine fuels and energy storage and transport. Ammobia’s “Haber-Bosch 2.0″ process will be the first ammonia technology in Lummus’ portfolio.

Lummus brings decades of experience in developing new technologies from initial concept to commercial scale, with expertise in reactor, process and thermal design. Combining Ammobia’s capital-efficient synthesis loop (“synloop”) with Lummus engineering and technology expertise and global reach provides a low-risk, financeable pathway to production for a variety of in-demand use cases such as power generation.

“Ammobia changes the economics of producing ammonia from any energy source and does it in modules rather than the world-scale plants that have defined this industry for a century,” said Karen Baert, Co-Founder and CEO of Ammobia. “Customers can add capacity through a greenfield project or an upgrade to an existing operating site. Lummus brings the engineering rigor, project delivery, and global relationships required to deploy it, which lets Ammobia stay focused on advancing the core process. Together we can make ammonia’s newest applications, from resilient power to clean maritime fuel, commercially viable.”

“We have a long track record of partnering with innovators to scale breakthrough technologies that address the evolving needs of the global energy market,” said Leon de Bruyn, President and Chief Executive Officer of Lummus Technology (Houston, Texas). “Ammobia’s technology is an important addition to Lummus’ portfolio and a leap forward for the industry. This cutting-edge solution has the power to transform ammonia production to be more economical and lower carbon, support emissions reductions in the shipping industry, and significantly reduce project costs.”

Ammonia demand is growing well beyond its traditional chemical uses. It already forms the foundation of 70% of fertilizers, which are responsible for feeding half the world’s population. Grand View Research projects ammonia production increasing 58% by 2033, driven by emerging demand as a maritime fuel and for power generation.

Ammobia’s technology is engineered to serve this full range of end markets. The Lummus partnership focuses on the energy generation opportunity, where the two companies will work together to bring projects to market at scale. Ammobia continues to advance its technology across ammonia’s other major segments, including fertilizer and industrial production.

text:
The Member of Parliament for Akuapem North, Sammi Awuku, says he will petition both the Minister of Transport and the International Maritime Organization over the handling of the vessel MV Sankofa, which passed through Ghana’s regulatory system last year despite being declared unseaworthy.

In a statement published on his Facebook page, the MP said he would write to Hon. Joseph Bukari Nikpe, the sector minister responsible for the Ghana Maritime Authority, and to the GMA Governing Board.

His requests, according to the statement, will cover the legal opinion, Board decision or other authority supporting the waiver of a US$1 million penalty imposed on the vessel; a full reconciliation of the pollution-related penalties; the identity and office of the person who authorised the vessel’s departure; and the inspection and clearance records relied upon in permitting it to sail.

He said he would also write to the International Maritime Organization. Where a vessel purports to sail under a flag that the named state says it never granted, he argued, it raises a fraudulent registration concern of precisely the kind the IMO tracks.

The matter, he said, did not begin or end in Ghanaian waters, and the inspection findings raise serious questions under international maritime safety and pollution-control standards.

The statement recounts that the Ghana Navy intercepted MV Sankofa off Axim on 22 July 2025 with its Automatic Identification System switched off.

A GMA inspection report dated 27 July 2025 recorded fourteen missing statutory certificates and the absence of an oil record book, garbage record book and sewage holding tank. São Tomé and Príncipe, the purported flag state, denied ever registering the vessel. The Authority concluded that it was not seaworthy.

The US$1 million statutory penalty was later waived, with GMA explaining that a subsequent inspection found no evidence the vessel had been trading in Ghana. The MP said that explanation does not resolve the matter.

The vessel was allowed to leave Ghana on 14 November 2025, reportedly under Cameroonian registration, and was later detained in Senegal in connection with a drug investigation while reportedly flying the Ghanaian flag.

“Ghana cannot shrug at this and then wonder why its flag reportedly appears on a vessel detained in a drug investigation in Dakar,” Awuku wrote.

text:
The government has set a target to raise the number of green-certified ship recycling yards in the country to more than 100 from the existing around 31, Industries, Commerce and Textiles and Jute Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said Monday.

“Several more yards are currently undergoing the process of obtaining green certification,” he said while addressing a workshop as the chief guest at Pan Pacific Sonargaon Hotel in the capital.

The Ministry of Industries and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) jointly organised the workshop to discuss the feasibility study report for establishing a Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility (TSDF) under the “Bangladesh Safe and Environmentally Sound Ship Recycling Project.”

The minister said Bangladesh is one of the leading countries in the global ship recycling industry and at one point surpassed India in terms of the tonnage of ships recycled.

“Although Bangladesh has fallen behind somewhat in recent times, its position in the global ship recycling industry remains significant,” he said.

Highlighting the economic importance of ship recycling, Muktadir said the sector provides employment to a large number of people and serves as an important source of scrap-the key raw material for the country’s steel industry.

However, he stressed that the sector must grow in a responsible and environmentally sound manner.

“Our goal is to make the industry more modern, safe and sustainable by complying with international conventions and environmental standards,” he said.

The minister emphasised the need for technical and financial assistance to increase the number of green-certified yards to over 100, alongside effective enforcement of environmental standards.

Referring to hazardous waste management as one of the major challenges in ship recycling, he said dismantling large vessels generates various hazardous materials and waste that can pose risks to the environment and public health if not properly managed.

He underscored the importance of a Treatment, Storage, and Disposal Facility (TSDF) for the safe and scientific collection, storage, treatment and disposal of such waste.

The proposed TSDF will play a significant role in managing a large portion of hazardous waste generated by the ship recycling industry, he said.

It will also create opportunities to manage hazardous waste from other sources, including industrial and electronic waste.

Such infrastructure would help bring the industry further in line with international environmental standards and enhance Bangladesh’s competitiveness in the global market, he added.

The minister said the ship recycling sector could be transformed into a safer, modern and sustainable industry through coordinated efforts by the government, industry owners, relevant institutions and international partners.

Industries Secretary Abdun Naser Khan chaired the workshop.

State Minister for the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change Shaikh Faridul Islam and Norwegian Ambassador to Bangladesh Hakon Arald Gulbrandsen also spoke at the workshop.

Sumiyuki Otsuki, an international expert from Japan Marine Science Company, presented the keynote paper.

description:
DP World has named its first methanol dual-fuel containership, DP World London, at a ceremony in Aarhus, Denmark.
DP World London joins Shipping Solutions fleet DP World London was built in China and delivered in April 2026.
Naming ceremony held in Aarhus DP World chose Aarhus for the naming ceremony because of the city’s connection with its Shipping Solutions business.
“This is a proud moment for our Shipping Solutions team,” said Martin Gaard Christiansen, CEO, Shipping Solutions EAM at DP World.
“This dual-fuel vessel reflects both our heritage and the future we are building.” The introduction of DP World London follows the recent addition of DP World Indus to DP World’s coastal shipping fleet in India.
text:
DP World has named its first methanol dual-fuel containership, DP World London, at a ceremony in Aarhus, Denmark.

The 1,250 TEU vessel will operate on a North Europe service. Its introduction marks another step in DP World’s investment in lower-emission maritime transport.

DP World London joins Shipping Solutions fleet

DP World London was built in China and delivered in April 2026.

The vessel is owned by Germany’s Elbdeich Reederei. DP World’s Shipping Solutions business operates the ship under the Portuguese flag.

The containership is 148 metres long and has a capacity of 1,250 TEUs.

It is equipped with a five-cylinder main engine and can operate using methanol. The vessel also features Exhaust Gas Recirculation technology to help reduce emissions.

First methanol bunkering completed in Rotterdam

The vessel completed its first methanol bunkering in Rotterdam on 25 June 2026.

Unibarge was the bunkering partner, while Methanex supplied the methanol.

DP World said the new vessel will support its efforts to offer more sustainable shipping solutions.

“The future of maritime trade will be shaped by resilience, connectivity and more sustainable transport solutions,” said Ganesh Raj, Global Chief Operating Officer, Marine Services at DP World.

He said the new vessel demonstrates DP World’s investment in practical technologies that can provide lower-emission transport.

Naming ceremony held in Aarhus

DP World chose Aarhus for the naming ceremony because of the city’s connection with its Shipping Solutions business.

The operation was founded in Aarhus as Unifeeder in 1977. It has since developed into a feeder and shortsea operator serving Europe and other markets.

Today, Shipping Solutions forms part of DP World’s wider Marine Services business.

“This is a proud moment for our Shipping Solutions team,” said Martin Gaard Christiansen, CEO, Shipping Solutions EAM at DP World.

“This dual-fuel vessel reflects both our heritage and the future we are building.”

The introduction of DP World London follows the recent addition of DP World Indus to DP World’s coastal shipping fleet in India.

The partnership was marked by the launch of a regional training program in Accra, designed to close competency gaps among seafarer certification examiners through a five-day workshop based on IMO Model Course 3.12: Assessment, Examination, and Certification of Seafarers.

Speaking at the opening, the Deputy Director General of the GMA, Mubarick Masawudu, noted the heavy responsibility resting on assessors, stating that certification extends far beyond basic paperwork.

“A Certificate of Competency represents a pledge that must hold water internationally, which is why consistency and integrity in our assessment systems are non-negotiable,” Mr Masawudu said.

He warned that if one administration’s credentials lose credibility, the resulting distrust could undermine the region’s standing in the global shipping industry.

Mr Masawudu said Ghana is determined to avoid such pitfalls by proactively strengthening assessor qualifications and examination frameworks well ahead of the IMO Member State Audit Scheme (IMSAS) in 2027.

The Deputy Director General also mentioned that as the global maritime spotlight increasingly turns toward Africa, the economic potential of ocean transport demands rigorous preparation and unwavering reliability.

“With the industry evolving rapidly each day, ensuring that every operational rope is tightly secured has never been more critical,” he said.

He added that raising the bar for the workforce through comprehensive training is not optional but essential for sustaining reliability and growth.

Mr Masawudu encouraged participants to use the workshop for honest self-reflection, scrutinising current practices, resolving inconsistencies, and adapting standards to meet evolving industry demands.

IMO Regional Representative for West and Central Africa, Capt. Dallas Laryea, reinforced that seafarer competence remains the cornerstone of maritime safety, security, and environmental protection.

He noted that as shipping undergoes rapid transformation driven by automation, digitalisation, and alternative fuels, strengthening certification credibility is more important than ever.

“This evolution requires future-ready seafarers equipped with a broad range of competencies, spanning from traditional seamanship to cyber awareness and the safe handling of new energy sources,” he said.

DP World’s Marine Services business, Shipping Solutions, has named its first methanol dual-fuel vessel, DP World London, at a ceremony in Aarhus, Denmark, as the company continues to invest in its fleet and lower-emission maritime transport.

The 1,250-TEU container vessel was built in China and delivered in April 2026. Owned by Germany’s Elbdeich Reederei and operated by DP World’s Shipping Solutions business, the Portugal-flagged vessel will operate on the North Europe service.

The 148-metre vessel is equipped with a five-cylinder main engine and Exhaust Gas Recirculation (EGR) technology to reduce emissions and support compliance with international environmental standards. It completed its first methanol bunkering in Rotterdam on 25 June 2026, with Unibarge as the bunkering partner and Methanex supplying the methanol.

The naming ceremony was held in Aarhus, where DP World’s Shipping Solutions business began in 1977 as Unifeeder. The business has since grown into a feeder and shortsea operator serving customers across Europe and beyond and is now part of DP World’s integrated Marine Services portfolio.

Martin Gaard Christiansen, CEO, Shipping Solutions EAM, DP World, said the vessel reflects the company’s heritage in Aarhus and its plans for fleet modernisation.

Ganesh Raj, Global Chief Operating Officer, Marine Services, DP World, said the methanol dual-fuel vessel is an example of the company’s investment in practical innovation and more reliable, flexible and lower-emission shipping solutions.

The vessel naming comes as DP World continues to expand its maritime and logistics network. The company reported a 13.1% increase in revenue to $12.7 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with $11.2 billion in the first half of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA reached $2.9 billion, with a margin of 22.5%.

DP World handled 42.8 million TEUs on a gross basis during the first half of 2026. Overall gross container volumes declined by 5.7% during the period, mainly because of temporary shipping disruptions at Jebel Ali Port. Excluding Jebel Ali, container volumes increased by 5.4% on a reported basis and 6.5% on a like-for-like basis.

The company invested $1.5 billion in capital expenditure during the first six months of 2026, with investments focused on capacity expansion in markets including the UK, India, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Saudi Arabia and Senegal. DP World expects full-year capital expenditure to be around $3 billion.

As part of its wider network expansion, DP World also reached an agreement in principle with the Fujairah Ports Authority for a 50-year concession to develop two terminals on the UAE’s east coast. The project includes the Al Rugaylat container and multi-purpose terminal and the Dibba General Cargo terminal.

Al Rugaylat is planned to handle up to 2.5 million TEUs of containers, 1.7 million tonnes of general cargo and 190,000 car equivalent units a year. Dibba will add up to 3.6 million tonnes of annual general cargo capacity. Once operational, the terminals are expected to increase DP World’s UAE container handling capacity from 19.4 million TEUs to almost 22 million TEUs.

The Fujairah terminals will be connected to Jebel Ali through DP World’s inland logistics network and integrated with Jafza. The project will be developed in phases, with construction expected to take around 24 to 30 months from commencement.

The BNP government has set a target to raise the number of green-certified ship recycling yards in the country to at least 100 from 31, Industries and Commerce Minister Khandakar Abdul Muktadir said on Monday.

He noted that currently several more shipbreaking yards are undergoing green certification.

Muktadir made the remarks as chief guest at a workshop jointly organised by the Ministry of Industries and the International Maritime Organization (IMO) at a hotel in the capital's Karwan Bazar.

The workshop was held to discuss a feasibility study report on setting up a Treatment, Storage and Disposal Facility (TSDF) centre under the "Bangladesh Safe and Environment-Friendly Ship Recycling Project."

Muktadir said Bangladesh remains one of the world's leading countries in ship recycling, having once surpassed even India in tonnage terms. "Although the country has slipped somewhat in recent times, it still holds a significant position in the global ship recycling industry."

Calling the sector vital to the national economy, the minister said it provides employment for a large number of people, while scrap from ships serves as a key raw material source for the country's steel industry.

He stressed that the sector's growth must be ensured in a responsible and environment-friendly manner, adding that the government's goal is to make the industry more modern, safe and sustainable through compliance with international conventions and environmental standards.

To take the number of green-certified yards to a hundred-plus, the minister emphasised technical and financial support alongside effective enforcement of environmental compliance requirements.

Describing hazardous waste management as one of the biggest challenges in ship recycling, Muktadir said large ships generate various hazardous materials and waste during dismantling, which, if not properly managed, pose risks to the environment and public health.

He said the proposed TSDF would play a key role in safely and scientifically collecting, storing, treating and disposing of such waste.

The proposed TSDF is expected to handle a major share of hazardous waste from the ship recycling industry, while also creating scope for managing hazardous waste from other industrial sources, including e-waste.

The minister expressed hope that the facility would help align the sector with international environmental standards and enhance Bangladesh's competitiveness in the global market.

He said a coordinated effort involving the government, yard owners, relevant institutions and international partners could transform the ship recycling sector into a safer, more modern and sustainable industry.
